Key Characteristics & Etiology: Infection of lung parenchyma; S. pneumoniae most common bacterial pathogen beyond neonatal period; RSV/viral in <2y
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Alveolar inflammation fluid exudation and consolidation impairing gas exchange
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Fever cough tachypnea chest retractions crackles; Red Flags: SpO2 <92% grunting lethargy inability to feed
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CXR lobar consolidation FBC leukocytosis elevated CRP; Oral Amoxicillin 1st line outpatient (IV Co-amoxiclav/Cefuroxime if severe)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Reversible lower airway inflammation and bronchospasm triggered by viral URTIs allergens cold air or exercise
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Eosinophilic mucosal edema airway hyperresponsiveness and smooth muscle constriction
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Dyspnea tachypnea polyphonic wheezing prolonged expiration intercostal retractions; Red Flags: Silent chest cyanosis PEF <33% confusion
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: SpO2 monitoring PEF measurement VBG pCO2 retention; Inhaled Salbutamol + Ipratropium via spacer/neb + Oral Prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg) + IV MgSO4

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute viral infection of upper airway peaking between 6 months and 3 years; Parainfluenza virus type 1 most common
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Subglottic mucosal edema and inflammation causing anatomical narrowing of upper airway
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Barking seal-like cough hoarseness inspiratory stridor sternal retractions; Red Flags: Stridor at rest severe agitation cyanosis
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis Neck XR steeple sign; Single dose Oral Dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg) for ALL + Nebulized L-Adrenaline if severe

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Severe life-threatening bacterial cellulitis of supraglottic structures; Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) primary cause
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Rapid supraglottic edema causing high-grade airway resistance and fatal airway obstruction
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden high fever severe sore throat drooling dysphagia tripoding posture stridor; Red Flags: Complete airway occlusion (DO NOT examine throat)
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Lateral neck XR thumbprint sign blood culture; Secure airway urgently in OT + IV Ceftriaxone

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Accidental inhalation of organic or inorganic foreign body into tracheobronchial tree (most common right main bronchus)
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mechanical airway occlusion causing air-trapping atelectasis or distal suppurative infection
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden choking paroxysmal cough persistent monophonic wheeze unilateral diminished breath sounds; Red Flags: Asphyxia silent chest
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Expiratory chest XR ball-valve emphysema; Rigid Bronchoscopy under general anesthesia (diagnostic and therapeutic)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis via airborne droplet inhalation from infectious adult contact
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Primary Ghon focus + lymphangitis + caseating hilar lymphadenopathy (Ghon complex)
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Persistent cough >2 weeks unexplained fever weight loss/failure to thrive night sweats; Red Flags: Respiratory distress hemoptysis
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Mantoux test (>=5mm in high risk >=10mm general) GeneXpert on gastric washings CXR lymphadenopathy; 2RHZE / 4RH (6 months total)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Hematogenous dissemination of M. tuberculosis from primary pulmonary focus
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Gelatinous basilar exudate entrapping cranial nerves (III VI VII) and causing vasculitis of circle of Willis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Prodrome fever irritability neck stiffness ptosis cranial nerve palsies seizures; Red Flags: Deep coma opisthotonos hemiplegia
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CSF: high protein low glucose (<0.3 ratio) lymphocytic pleocytosis GeneXpert positive; 12-month Anti-TB (RHZE) + IV Dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Severe systemic IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity reaction triggered by foods (peanuts nuts) insect stings or drugs
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Massive systemic histamine and cytokine release causing vasodilation bronchospasm and capillary leak
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Acute urticaria angioedema wheezing dyspnea stridor vomiting abdominal cramps hypotension/shock; Red Flags: Respiratory arrest vascular collapse
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis serum tryptase level; Immediate Intramuscular Adrenaline 1:1,000 (0.01 mg/kg or 0.15mg <6y 0.3mg 6-12y) in anterolateral thigh

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute viral lower respiratory infection in infants <12 months; Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) primary pathogen (>75%)
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Small airway viral necrosis epithelial shedding mucosal edema and mucus plugging causing air-trapping
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Coryza low-grade fever tachypnea intercostal retractions bilateral expiratory wheeze and fine polyphonic crackles; Red Flags: Apnea SpO2 <92% poor feeding
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis RSV nasopharyngeal aspirate PCR; Supportive care (supplemental O2 if SpO2 <92% and feeding/hydration support)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Highly contagious respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis gram-negative coccobacillus
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Pertussis toxin damages ciliated respiratory epithelium causing severe paroxysmal coughing and systemic lymphocytosis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Paroxysmal coughing fits ending in high-pitched inspiratory whoop post-tussive emesis; Red Flags: Apneic attacks in young infants
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Full blood count: marked leukocytosis with absolute lymphocytosis PCR/nasopharyngeal swab; Oral Azithromycin for 5 days
